masthead_title: Thursday’s rally was broad but skipped AI hardware, and junk-bond spreads widened on Wednesday’s selloff day.
regime_line: Bond yields fell (the 10-year down 9bp to 5.10%) despite a much hotter producer-price report, the equal-weight S&P 500 (every stock counted the same) rose 1.37% while AI hardware kept falling, and junk-bond spreads printed 3.25% for Wednesday’s selloff day, wider than on any day in the past six months (tightening).
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — two resolved (both confirmed), two open, two new

Every open conditional claim (§4B — a specific, falsifiable test this system logs before the outcome is known, then grades against the data) is checked against the latest closes and prints before any new narrative is written. Prices are Yahoo closes and credit prints recorded in data/raw/claims_check_2026-10-16.json.

  • CL-0043 confirmed — if Wednesday was a risk event rather than a rotation, credit would say so on the day. The test needed the high-yield spread print (HY OAS, the extra yield on junk-rated bonds) dated 10-14 to come in at 3.21% or wider. It came in at 3.25%, up 9bp from 3.16%. Confirmed: on the selloff day, junk-bond lenders asked for more, not less.
  • CL-0038 confirmed — Coherent’s 10-08 optics selloff as a genuine re-rating (a lasting reset in what investors will pay), not a one-day overreaction. Coherent’s best close in the window was $312.62 (+3.40%), short of the $317.47 refute line. It ended the window at $250.60 on Thursday, 17.12% below the $302.35 base. No outlet reported a company-specific reason for Thursday’s 4.83% fall.
  • CL-0042 open — Wednesday’s AI-hardware selloff as the start of a durable repricing. The chip fund SMH closed Thursday at $558.84, below the $564.74 confirm line and far from the $588.12 refute line. Confirmation needs a close at or below $564.74 on Wednesday 10-21 with no refute close first. Graded on the 2026-10-22 run.
  • CL-0041 open, confirmation out of reach — last Thursday’s junk-spread widening as the start of credit repricing. Prints dated 10-09 to 10-14: 3.11%, 3.11%, 3.16%, 3.25%. Only a print at or below 3.03% refutes it, and the last print in its window (dated 10-15) arrives Monday. Otherwise it expires. Graded on the 2026-10-19 run.
  • Reported, not graded: the withdrawn CL-0044. Yesterday’s edition withdrew an event-day test of whether the 2-year would move with Thursday’s data surprise, because yields were already falling overnight. As promised, the outcome is reported without a grade. Both prints beat consensus: producer prices +1.3% on the month (calendar consensus +0.5%) and retail sales +0.8% (+0.3%), per CNBC and Reuters. The 2-year still fell 5bp, to 4.77%.
  • CL-0045 opens — Thursday’s rotation out of the biggest AI names into the rest of the market continues. Test: the equal-weight RSP (the average S&P stock) beats the cap-weighted SPY from Thursday’s closes ($215.00 and $771.79) through Thursday 10-22’s close (confirms); SPY ahead by 1.0 point or more refutes it; SPY ahead by less than a point expires. story_html:
The press calls Thursday a rotation away from AI. CNBC’s live blog led with “Dow rises more than 500 points as investors rotate away from AI trade.” Reuters’ close: “S&P 500 ends higher as traders shift from AI to healthcare.” The Associated Press: “Wall Street muscles higher despite more swings for AI stocks.” On bonds, CNBC headlined “Treasury yields slide as investors flee to safety of bonds amid tech rout.” That came on a day the data ran hot. The producer price index (PPI, prices businesses get paid) rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, the biggest gains since 2022, per CNBC and Reuters reporting of the government release; this system’s calendar had +0.5% for the month. Core PPI (excluding food and energy) rose 0.7% against a 0.3% calendar consensus. Retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected; Reuters said higher gasoline prices drove the beat. Yahoo Finance summed up the puzzle: “The PPI Was Much Higher Than Expected. Odds of a Fed Rate Hike Edged Down Anyway.” This morning CNBC leads with “S&P 500 futures are little changed as index heads for losing week,” and AP headlined Asia’s session “Stocks rebound after tech sell-off and Indonesia shares sink on market downgrade warning.” The Wall Street Journal’s and Financial Times’ own pages couldn’t be reached from this system’s search, so their framing isn’t reported.

What the data shows: bonds rallied on hot data. The 10-year fell 9bp to 5.10% and the 30-year 9bp, while the 2-year fell 5bp. Per CME Group’s own FedWatch account, the odds of an October hike “dropped below 30%” by Thursday afternoon, after peaking near 53% following Wednesday’s CPI; around the PPI release they were near 34% (Schwab, CNBC). So hot inflation data came with lower yields and lower hike odds. CNBC’s explanation is a flight to safety from tech stocks; that is CNBC’s reading, and this system can’t separate it from other explanations with one day of data. The 10-year has been at or above 5.10% since Sep 23. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007 (Today in history, below).

On stocks, the data says “broad” this time, but not for AI hardware. The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to 7,744.06, its first gain in four sessions, 0.96% below its Oct 6 record. The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.08%. The average S&P stock (equal-weight RSP) rose 1.37%, against 0.28% for the cap-weighted SPY, and the Russell 2000 rose 1.38%. But the chip fund SMH fell 1.04%, its eighth straight daily decline. Software, homebuilders and health care rose; AI hardware fell again (Movers, below). Over the week, the average stock is up 0.92% while the index is down 0.87%.

The Fed goes quiet after today. Speaking with the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok (late Thursday, U.S. time), Fed Chair Warsh gave no signal on October. CNBC headlined “Fed’s Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with ‘no free riders,’” and quoted him: “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” CNBC also reported him saying AI’s path will be “very bumpy.” The Fed’s pre-meeting quiet period runs Oct 17–29 (Chicago Fed calendar), so today is the last day officials can comment before the Oct 27–28 meeting.

Oil is still the inflation story. WTI rose 3.03% Thursday to $97.97, up 6.66% this week. A wire report carried by Nation Thailand tied the gain to an 8.6-million-barrel weekly drop in U.S. crude inventories reported by the Energy Information Administration; that is one outlet’s stated reason, not checked against a second source. Energy stocks fell 1.58% anyway, and no outlet this system found explained the split. This morning Reuters reported oil edging lower as the U.S. weighs easing sanctions on “shadow fleet” tankers carrying non-sanctioned oil, a proposal still under discussion. Why this matters: energy ran through both of Thursday’s hot numbers. Reuters said energy made up most of the jump in producer goods prices, and that gas stations made up roughly 70% of September’s retail-sales gain, with sales excluding gasoline up only about 0.2%. For households that means pump prices, not a broad pickup in spending.
dashboard_interp_html:
Long-term rates fell more than short-term rates. The 10-year fell 9bp to 5.10% (z +1.60) and the 30-year 9bp to 5.43% (z +1.31, no longer flagged). The 2-year fell 5bp to 4.77% (z +1.75) and the 3-month bill held at 4.28% (z +2.29). Because long-term yields fell more, the curve flattened: the 2s10s spread (the 10-year minus the 2-year) narrowed 4bp to 33bp, and 18bp over five sessions. Falling yields with a flatter curve is a bull flattener (Unit 1). The 2-year, which tracks where traders expect the Fed’s rate to go, fell less (5bp), in line with the lower October hike odds in the story above.

High against the last 30 years, average against the full record. The 3-month bill sits at the 53rd percentile since 1981 and the 71st over the last 30 years. The 2-year sits at the 52nd percentile since 1976 and the 82nd over 30 years. The 10-year sits at the 47th percentile since 1962 and the 84th over 30 years. The 30-year sits at the 47th percentile since 1977 and the 83rd over 30 years. Every maturity is in the upper part of its last-30-years range (71st to 84th percentile) and near the middle of its full record (47th to 53rd).

Wednesday’s real-yield split filled in. On CPI day the 10-year fell 2bp. The 10-year real yield (what a Treasury pays after inflation, dated 10-14) fell 4bp to 2.84%, and the 10-year breakeven (the bond market’s inflation forecast) rose 2bp to 2.35%. So on CPI day the bond market’s inflation forecast rose a little while real yields fell (Unit 2). Thursday’s split arrives Monday.

Credit widened on the selloff day. HY OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies, dated 10-14) rose 9bp to 3.25% (z +3.73, the day’s largest flag). That’s wider than on any day in the past six months, just above Oct 1’s 3.24%. It sits at the 77th percentile of its own ~3-year record here: unusual lately, upper-middle on its short full record. IG OAS (the investment-grade version, dated 10-14) rose 1bp to 0.84% (z +1.91). That print confirms CL-0043 (Claims, above). Thursday’s credit print, the rally day, arrives Monday.

The dollar (DXY, z +1.66) fell 0.54% to 102.00: the 71st percentile since 1971 and the 80th over 30 years. SOFR (the overnight bank funding rate, dated 10-14) was 3.88% (z +2.25). It reads high against six months because it stepped up at the Fed’s September hike, from 3.62% to 3.85%, and has stayed between 3.85% and 3.90% since. This week’s Fed balance-sheet report (H.4.1, dated 10-14) showed the balance sheet up $8.1 billion to $6.756 trillion and the Treasury’s cash account (TGA) up $3.1 billion to $883.4 billion. ON RRP (money funds’ overnight parking spot at the Fed) was $1.20 billion on Thursday. All small moves (Friday liquidity panel, in Tier 3).

Why this matters: the 10-year is down 14bp this week, and mortgage rates tend to follow it, so home buyers got a small break in a week of hot inflation data. Savers still earn high short-term rates: the 3-month bill hasn’t budged. And for bond-fund holders, credit is the piece to watch: junk-bond spreads are wider than at any point in six months.
history_html:
The level, and the run. The 10-year fell to 5.10%, below this run’s 5.31% peak of Oct 5, but it has been at or above 5.10% since Sep 23. Before this run, it was last there in July 2007. Against the last 30 years that’s high (84th percentile); since 1962 it’s average (47th).

July 2007, then vs. now. Long-term rates match: 5.11% then, 5.10% now, with similar real yields, breakevens and term premium (a Fed model’s estimate of the extra yield for lending long). Short-term rates don’t. The Fed’s rate was 5.25% then; SOFR is 3.88% now, so the 3-month-to-10-year spread is +82bp against +14bp then. And the S&P 500 was at a record that day; today it’s 0.96% below one.

The speed is in two-year yields. The 2-year is up 130bp this year, the 8th-largest rise through this date in 50 years. A 12-month rise this big (1.27 points) has started 8 times since 1977. From each start, stocks were lower a year later in 3 of 8, against 24.4% for any 12-month stretch. A recession began within two years in 2 of 8, against 27.4% normally. Eight is a small sample.

Credit, on the longest record. Junk spreads here have only a three-year record. The long-run proxy (Baa corporate yields minus the 10-year, dated 10-06) sits at the 3rd percentile since 1986 and the 2nd over 30 years: still tight. This week’s widening is real, but short-term.

Why this matters (client-ready): “Long-term rates are back at mid-2007 levels, and junk-bond spreads just passed anything in six months, but on the longest record, corporate borrowing spreads are still tight. When two-year rates rose this fast before, stocks were lower a year later in 3 of 8 cases, versus about one in four normally: a small sample, not a forecast.”
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically (503 of 503 covered, plus all 50 megacaps); a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest), never by seeming interesting. 83 name candidates and 3 sector divergences qualified; cap is 3 names + 1 sector note. Left out: Equifax (+7.25%) and FICO (+6.99%), the scan’s largest gains, with no reported catalyst. Marsh McLennan (+4.56%) was the day’s one earnings reaction: AP reported it rose after a stronger-than-expected profit. Other insurance brokers rose too, but no outlet linked them, so no read-through is claimed. International Paper, Reddit and Coinbase had no reported reason.

ServiceNow (NOW) +6.14% (148.57, from 139.98) — what happened: it led a broad software rally: Intuit +6.36%, Autodesk +6.07%, Adobe +4.57%, Salesforce +4.57%, Workday +4.16%. Stated reason: Invezz reported that TD Cowen raised its price target to $165 from $140 and reiterated Buy. Invezz and Benzinga both framed the day as investors rotating out of heavily indebted AI names into established enterprise software; no outlet extended the TD Cowen note to the other names. Read-through: inside tech, Thursday’s split followed the outlets’ financing story: names tied to debt-funded data-center building fell, while enterprise software rose. That’s the outlets’ framing, which one day can’t test; CL-0045 tests whether the broader rotation lasts.

Dell (DELL) −6.80% (473.39, from 507.93) — what happened: a second straight drop, 17.31% in two sessions. HPE fell 7.10% (14.79% in two sessions), Arista 5.04% and Coherent 4.83%. Stated reason: no new company news turned up. Reuters described the declines as adding to the prior session’s losses amid worries about AI companies’ exposure to higher borrowing costs. Wednesday’s Barclays downgrade said a meaningful AI-driven growth inflection had yet to emerge (Stocktwits, The Fly). Read-through: cycle-level. Reuters’ framing links hardware makers to their customers’ borrowing costs: if data-center builders pay more to borrow, orders for servers and networking gear are what’s at risk. A hypothesis, tested at the cycle level through CL-0042.

Lennar (LEN) +5.66% (77.69, from 73.53) — what happened: homebuilders led a rate-sensitive rally: D.R. Horton +4.42%, Home Depot +4.31%. Stated reason: Yahoo Finance’s live blog grouped the homebuilder gains with the drop in Treasury yields and a rotation out of tech; that is Yahoo’s framing. Read-through: the rates channel to housing. Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year, which fell 9bp Thursday and 14bp this week, so a lower 10-year is the one piece of good news for builders in a week of hot inflation data. (Lennar was the subject of CL-0033, which expired unresolved in yesterday’s edition; it now sits above that claim’s $74.44 base.)

Sector note — Health Care (XLV) +1.86% vs. SPY +0.28% (+1.57 points); Energy (XLE) −1.58% (−1.87 points). Materials (XLB, +1.79%) also beat the market. Reuters’ closing headline framed the day as traders shifting from AI to health care; health care also led on Wednesday (+2.53%). Energy fell even though WTI rose 3%, and no outlet this system found explained that split. Read-through: two days of health-care leadership fit a defensive tilt; energy’s break from oil is unexplained and is a watch item, not a signal.
chart_of_day_why: Mechanical rule (§6.5a, largest |z| flag) points to HY OAS again: z +3.73, dated 10-14, ahead of the 3-month bill’s +2.29 and SOFR’s +2.25. Yesterday’s chart set up the question; today’s print answers it. The selloff-day reading came in at 3.25%, confirming CL-0043, just above Oct 1’s 3.24% (marked). For §4F scale: 3.25% sits at the 77th percentile of the high-yield spread’s ~3-year record here, so it’s unusual against the past six months but not extreme on its short full record.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (this system’s chip-fund proxy for AI capex) fell 1.04% against SPY’s +0.28%, its eighth straight daily decline. It is down 7.37% this week and 16.46% below its Jun 22 six-month high.

Weekly financing-cycle note (Friday, §5). The week split the AI cycle in two. Demand looked strong. TSMC, the chipmaker that builds most AI processors, reported third-quarter net income of NT$763.06 billion, up 68.7% from a year earlier (company filing, Oct 15), above the roughly NT$740.8 billion consensus cited in pre-results coverage. It guided fourth-quarter revenue to $52.3–54.3 billion and kept its 2026 capital budget at $60–64 billion, the range it set in July (Motley Fool call transcript). Financing looked strained. CNBC reported CoreWeave’s bond yields near 15% on Wednesday, and Reuters, citing LSEG, put its credit default swaps (insurance against a default) above 1,000bp. Reuters reported Oracle’s five-year swaps at a record 288bp after Wednesday’s session, and Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia at record wides, far below Oracle’s; those contracts trade thinly. Deals got harder: AirTrunk put its roughly $1.5 billion Singapore REIT listing on hold after considering a higher yield (The Star, citing Bloomberg, Oct 14). Volta marketed about $5 billion of data-center debt at yields of at least 11%, with no final pricing reported (Semafor). Stack Infrastructure is seeking about $6 billion for a Melbourne site (Bloomberg). On volume, Bloomberg counted nearly $500 billion of AI-related borrowing priced in 2026 as of Oct 8, and the IMF said hyperscalers now make up about 10% of global investment-grade issuance, up from under 1% in 2024 (Reuters). No hyperscaler changed its capex guidance this week.

Cycle-level reading: the supplier reports record profit while the borrowers pay more. That is the shape the Lucent watch (§5) exists for: a supplier’s results looking strong while its customers’ financing gets harder. This week fits the shape, not the outcome; it is a watch item, not a verdict (§8: cycle-level only). The map below puts the cycle in history: IT investment and corporate stock values are both record shares of GDP, while corporate debt is still below its 2020 high. Why this matters: for a client in AI-related stocks, the risk to watch is the cost of credit for the builders, not the chip orders. CL-0042 and CL-0046 track both pieces.

Friday liquidity panel (§9) — Fed balance sheet, TGA, ON RRP and SOFR over the trailing window. The balance sheet and TGA remain “thin history” per §4 pending 60 weekly observations. This week’s moves were small; SOFR shows the September hike step and a narrow 3.85%–3.90% range since.
calendar_note_html:
Today: September import prices (8:30am ET; consensus +0.6% on the month, prior +0.7%), industrial production (9:15am; +0.4% after a flat August) and capacity utilization (76.5%, prior 76.3%), the federal budget (2pm) and foreign flows into U.S. securities (TIC, 4pm), per this system’s calendar. Truist reported before the open: adjusted earnings of $1.16 a share, up 12% from a year earlier, against a $1.13 consensus (company filing; Benzinga consensus). After Thursday’s close, CNBC’s roundup listed Interactive Brokers, J.B. Hunt and Alcoa moving on results. The Fed’s quiet period starts Saturday (Oct 17–29, Chicago Fed calendar).

Thursday’s results: PPI +1.3% on the month and +6.3% on the year; core +0.7% (CNBC, Reuters). Retail sales +0.8% (Reuters). Jobless claims 199,000 for the week ended Oct 10, against 195,000 in the calendar (Labor Department, via Seeking Alpha). The Philadelphia Fed’s factory index fell to 20.9 from 37.8, below the 26.5 consensus but still positive, meaning activity is still growing; new orders dropped to 4.3 (Philadelphia Fed).

Why this matters to the current regime: the inflation numbers ran hot, but the activity numbers are cooling at the edges: the Philly Fed’s new orders nearly stalled, and retail sales were mostly gasoline. Today’s industrial production is the next read on factories. For clients, that mix (hot prices, softer activity) is the hardest one for the Fed and for bond funds.
concept_unit: Unit 6 — Positioning & sentiment vs. fundamentals, segment 2
concept_title: Rotation or retreat? Two days, two breadth readings
concept_html: Segment 1 introduced breadth: the index versus the average stock. Thursday is Wednesday’s mirror image. On Wednesday SPY (cap-weighted) fell 1.08% and RSP (equal-weight) fell 0.57%. On Thursday SPY rose 0.28% and RSP rose 1.37%. Over the two days, SPY is down 0.80% and RSP is up 0.80%. That is what a rotation looks like: money moving between groups of stocks (out of the biggest AI names, into software, homebuilders and health care), not money leaving stocks. A retreat looks different: most stocks fall together, and the worry shows up in credit. Here is the complication. Credit did react: junk-bond spreads widened 9bp on Wednesday’s selloff day (CL-0043, confirmed). So the honest reading is mostly rotation, with a credit warning attached, and the warning sits where the debt is: AI builders that borrowed heavily. Unit 6’s question applies too. A rotation changes which companies investors favor. It doesn’t, by itself, say the economy changed.
client_translation: The market didn’t really go up or down this week so much as shuffle: money left the most popular AI stocks and spread into everything else, which is why an evenly spread portfolio held up better than the headline index.
client_lens_html:
“Is inflation getting worse?” The September numbers say prices are rising faster: consumer prices up 3.7% from a year earlier (CNBC, Wednesday), and producer prices up 6.3%, the biggest gain since 2022 (CNBC, Reuters). Energy is the common thread. Gasoline was more than half of September’s consumer-price gain (CNBC), and Reuters tied most of the retail-sales gain to gas stations. So the pain is real at the pump, but it isn’t yet a broad spending boom.

“Why did my tech fund fall when the market rose?” Money rotated. The chip fund SMH has fallen eight sessions in a row while software, homebuilders and health care rallied Thursday. This week the average S&P stock is up 0.92% while the index is down 0.87%. A fund concentrated in AI hardware felt the whole drop; the equal-weight fund is up 0.92% this week.

“Is the Fed raising rates in October?” Markets now lean against it, and the Fed isn’t saying. Chair Warsh declined to signal the decision on Thursday night (CNBC), and policymakers go quiet after today. Per CME Group’s FedWatch account, October hike odds fell below 30% on Thursday after peaking near 53% following CPI. The meeting is Oct 27–28. For savers, short-term yields stay high either way.
